steps.title: Internet & Web Fundamentals
steps.goal: After this step you can explain, in simple words, how a web page gets from a server to your screen.
topics: Clients and servers: your browser asks, a server answers
The parts of a web address (URL)
DNS: the phone book that turns a name into a number
HTTP: the question-and-answer rules of the web, and its status codes
HTTPS: locking the conversation so others cannot read it
Packets: how data is cut into small pieces and sent
checkpoint: Write down the story of opening a web page in order (name lookup, connection, request, page drawn) and compare it with the MDN page.
Say what the status codes 200, 301, 404 and 503 mean.
Explain in one sentence what DNS does.

practice.label: What happens when you type a URL

project.brief: Open your browser's network tab, load a website, and write down every request it makes: what was asked, what came back and the status code.

steps.title: HTML Basics
steps.goal: After this step you can build a well-structured page with headings, links, images, tables and forms that people using screen readers can also use.
topics: Headings, paragraphs and lists
Links and images
Page structure with meaningful tags (header, main, footer)
Tables and how to make them readable for everyone
Forms and buttons
Accessibility: making pages usable with a keyboard and a screen reader
Checking and fixing mistakes in your HTML
checkpoint: Build a page with a header, a main part and a footer using the right tags.
Make a form where every field has a label.
Explain why accessibility matters and name two things you do to support it.

project.brief: Build a one-page personal profile with headings, a photo with a text description, a table of your skills and a contact form. Use only HTML; the form does not need to send anything.

steps.title: CSS Advanced
steps.goal: After this step you can lay out a page with Flexbox and Grid so that it looks right on both a phone and a laptop.
topics: Selectors and the cascade: which style wins when two rules clash
The box model: content, padding, border and margin
Flexbox: lining things up in a row or a column
Grid: placing things in rows and columns
Responsive design: media queries that change the layout by screen size
Units and sizing
Backgrounds, borders and overflow
checkpoint: Center something on the page in both directions with Flexbox.
Build a three-column layout with Grid that becomes one column on a phone.
Explain which rule wins when two CSS rules point at the same thing.

project.brief: Rebuild your profile page so that it uses Flexbox for the header and Grid for a card section, and changes layout under 600 pixels wide.

steps.title: JavaScript Core
steps.goal: After this step you can write JavaScript that reacts to clicks, changes the page and loads data from a server.
topics: Variables, numbers, text, lists and objects
Making decisions (if) and repeating work (loops)
Functions
Events: reacting to clicks and typing
The DOM: reading and changing the page from code
Loading data from a server and reading JSON
Finding and fixing errors (debugging)
checkpoint: Write code that adds an item to a list on the page when a button is clicked.
Fetch data from a public API and show it on the page.
Use the browser's developer tools to find why a script fails.

project.brief: Build a to-do list that adds, ticks and removes items, and loads a joke or a quote from a public API when the page opens.

steps.title: React Basics
steps.goal: After this step you can build a small app from components that remember and show changing data.
topics: Components: small reusable pieces of a page
JSX: writing page structure inside JavaScript
Props: passing data into a component
State (useState): data a component remembers and shows
Showing things only sometimes, and showing lists
Handling clicks and typing
Thinking in React: splitting a design into components
checkpoint: Turn a page design into a tree of components and name the data each one needs.
Explain the difference between props and state.
Build a counter and a list that changes when you click.

project.brief: Rebuild your to-do list in React with a separate component for the list, an item and the add form.

steps.title: React Advanced
steps.goal: After this step you can share data across a React app, move between pages, and test a component the way a user would use it.
topics: Hooks: useState remembers data, useEffect runs code after the screen updates, useRef holds a value without redrawing, and you can write your own
Context: sharing data without passing it through every component
Reducers: one place that describes how data changes (React docs: Scaling Up with Reducer and Context)
Moving between pages with React Router
Making slow screens faster (useMemo, useCallback)
Testing a component by what the user sees (Testing Library)
checkpoint: Use context so that a theme choice is available in every component.
Add two pages with React Router and a link between them.
Write a test that clicks a button and checks what appears.

project.brief: Add a login page and a dashboard page to your React app. Keep the signed-in user in context and write two tests.

steps.title: CSS Frameworks
steps.goal: After this step you can style a responsive page with Tailwind CSS, including a dark mode.
topics: Why use utility classes: small classes you combine in your HTML
Installing Tailwind CSS with Vite
Responsive design: add a prefix like md: to change styling on bigger screens
Mobile first: plain classes apply to every screen, prefixes add changes
Dark mode with the dark: prefix
Customizing colors and breakpoints
checkpoint: Style a card that has one column on a phone and two columns on a tablet.
Add a dark mode that follows the visitor's system setting.
Explain what mobile first means.

project.brief: Restyle your React app with Tailwind CSS: a responsive layout and a dark mode switch.

steps.title: Next.js
steps.goal: After this step you can build a multi-page Next.js app that loads data on the server and can be put online.
topics: What Next.js adds to React
The App Router: pages and layouts made from folders
Linking between pages
Server components and client components
Loading data on the server and caching it
Refreshing saved pages (revalidating)
Route handlers: small pieces of server code that answer web addresses
Deploying a Next.js app
checkpoint: Create two pages and a shared layout using folders.
Explain in one sentence the difference between a server component and a client component.
Load data on the server and show it on a page, and add a route handler that returns JSON.

project.brief: Build a small blog in Next.js with a list page, a page for each post and a shared layout. Keep posts in a simple file.

steps.title: Production & Deployment
steps.goal: After this step you can put a site online, run automatic checks on every change, and measure how fast it feels to visitors.
topics: Git and GitHub basics: saving your work in steps (commits) and sending it to GitHub
Deploying from a GitHub repository to a service such as Vercel
Keeping passwords and keys in environment settings, not in code
Automatic checks on every push with GitHub Actions
Core Web Vitals: three numbers for loading speed, response time and layout jumps
Measuring speed with PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse
checkpoint: Put your app online with its secrets set as environment settings, and share the link.
Explain what a workflow (automatic checks that run when you push code) does.
Name the three Core Web Vitals and say what each one measures.

project.brief: Deploy your Next.js or React app, add a GitHub Actions workflow that builds it on every push, and write down its Core Web Vitals scores.

steps.title: OS & Networking Basics
steps.goal: After this step you can explain, in simple words, what happens between typing a web address and seeing the page.
topics: Clients and servers: your browser asks, a server answers
Processes and threads: how a computer runs many things at once
Ports and sockets: the numbered doors a program listens on
TCP and UDP: a careful way and a quick way to send data
DNS: the phone book that turns a name into a number (an IP address)
HTTP: the question-and-answer rules of the web, and its status codes like 200 and 404
HTTPS and TLS: locking the conversation so others cannot read it
checkpoint: Tell the story of opening a web page in order: name lookup, connection, lock, request, page drawn.
Say when you would pick TCP (careful) and when UDP (quick), with one example each.
Name five HTTP status codes and say what each one tells the browser.

practice.label: What happens when you type a URL

project.brief: Write a tiny web server with only the tools built into Node.js. It answers one address with some data and every other address with a 404 (not found). Test it with the curl command and read the headers.

steps.title: Node.js Fundamentals
steps.goal: After this step you can explain how Node.js serves many people with a single worker, and write programs that read files without freezing.
topics: What Node.js is: a way to run JavaScript outside the browser that does not wait around
The event loop: the worker's to-do list that keeps Node.js busy
Three ways to run code later: nextTick, setTimeout and setImmediate
Promises and async/await: a clean way to wait for slow work
Modules: splitting code into files (CommonJS and ES modules)
Files: reading and writing, and why the waiting kind freezes everything
Streams: handling big data a piece at a time
Buffers: raw bytes and text encodings
checkpoint: Explain why a file call that waits (a synchronous call) makes every other visitor wait too.
Read a large file with a stream, a piece at a time, instead of loading it all into memory.
Say that nextTick callbacks run first and setImmediate runs after the current work, and why too many nextTick calls can starve the loop.

project.brief: Build a command-line tool that reads a large text file a piece at a time and prints the ten most common words, without loading the whole file into memory.

steps.title: Express.js & Routing
steps.goal: After this step you can build a web API with Express where each address does one job and all errors are handled in one place.
topics: A minimal Express app
Routes: which code runs for which address and method (GET, POST and so on)
Reading request data: req.params (from the address), req.query (after the ?) and req.body (sent data)
Routers: grouping related routes in one file
Middleware: small steps a request passes through before the answer is sent
Built-in middleware: reading JSON, reading forms, serving files
Error handlers: one place that catches mistakes and sends a clean answer
Errors in async code, which Express 5 passes on for you
checkpoint: Build routes to create, read, update and delete items that answer 201 (created), 204 (done, nothing to send back) and 404 (not found) where they should.
Write an error handler, place it last, and explain why the order matters.
Explain what middleware does and what happens if it forgets to call next.

project.brief: Build a to-do list API that keeps items in a simple list in memory. Add a middleware that checks the data sent, and one error handler that returns a clean message.

steps.title: Database Design
steps.goal: After this step you can decide how to store related data, make searches fast with indexes, and write basic queries in MongoDB and SQL.
topics: Two ways to store data: tables (SQL) and documents (MongoDB)
CRUD: create, read, update and delete in MongoDB
Embedding or referencing: keep related data inside one record, or link to another record
Indexes: like a book's index, they make reading fast but make every write a little slower
Aggregation: asking questions about many records at once (filter, group, sort)
Mongoose: a helper that gives your MongoDB data a fixed shape
SQL basics: select, join, group by
Transactions: a group of changes that all happen or none happen
checkpoint: For a blog with posts and comments, choose to embed or to link, and give the reason in one sentence.
Explain how an index makes a search faster and what it costs every time you save data.
Write a query that counts the posts of each user and sorts the result.

project.brief: Build a blog API with users, posts and comments. Write down why you embedded or linked each part, add two indexes, and add one query that counts posts per user. Connect it to Express with Mongoose.

steps.title: Authentication & Security
steps.goal: After this step you can add sign-in to an API and say what each protection (hashing, cookies, headers, limits) guards against.
topics: Saving passwords safely: never the password itself, only a deliberately slow scrambled version with a random extra (a salt)
Sessions and tokens: how the site remembers you are signed in. A token (JWT) is signed so it cannot be changed, but anyone can read it
Cookie settings: Secure (only over HTTPS), HttpOnly (scripts cannot read it), SameSite (limits sending to other sites)
OAuth 2.0: how "Sign in with Google" lets one site act for you without your password
CORS: a rule the browser follows about which websites may call your API. Other tools such as curl ignore it
Authorization: checking who is allowed to do what
Checking all input and stopping injection (tricking the database with specially written input)
Hardening: security headers (Helmet), limits on tries per minute, and checking your packages for known problems
checkpoint: Explain why passwords are scrambled with a slow method and a salt, and not just locked with a key.
Say what is inside a token (JWT) and why you must never put secrets in it.
Explain why CORS does not stop someone using the curl tool.

project.brief: Add register and login to your API. Scramble the passwords, keep the login in an HttpOnly cookie, limit login tries, add Helmet, and check that one user cannot read another user's data.

steps.title: Testing & Debugging
steps.goal: After this step you can write tests that check your API automatically, and use the Node.js debugger to find a bug.
topics: Unit tests (one small piece) and integration tests (pieces working together)
The test tool built into Node.js: describe, it and subtests
Testing web routes with supertest, which sends fake requests to your app
Skipping tests and checking how much code the tests cover
Setup and cleanup steps, and a separate test database so real data is safe
Keeping the app separate from the part that starts the server, so tests can use it
Debugging: pausing the program with --inspect and looking inside
Trying an API by hand with Postman
checkpoint: Write a test for a route with supertest that checks the status code and the data returned.
Start Node.js with --inspect and stop on a breakpoint (a line where the program pauses).
Say the difference between a unit test and an integration test, and when each is worth writing.

practice.label: Status codes you check in tests

project.brief: Write ten tests for your Express API, including a not-found case, a bad-input case and a failed login (this needs the login from the previous step). Run them with node --test.

steps.title: Docker & Containers
steps.goal: After this step you can pack an API into an image, run it as a container, and start it together with a database using one command.
topics: Containers and virtual machines: a container shares the computer's core, so it is lighter
Images and containers: the image is the recipe, the container is the running dish
The Dockerfile: the list of steps that builds an image
docker build and docker run, and linking a port of your computer to the container
Volumes: a safe place so database files survive a restart
.dockerignore: files you do not want to copy into the image
Docker Compose: several containers described in one file and started together
Passing settings in as environment variables
checkpoint: Write a Dockerfile for your API and run it with a port linked to your computer.
Explain the difference between an image and a container.
Use Compose to start the API and MongoDB together.

project.brief: Pack your API and MongoDB with Docker Compose, so that one command starts both and all settings come from environment variables.

steps.title: Deployment & Cloud
steps.goal: After this step you can put an API on the internet from GitHub, keep secrets out of your code, and run your tests automatically on every push.
topics: Keeping passwords and keys in environment settings, never in the code
Automatic checks on every push with GitHub Actions: workflows, triggers, jobs and runners
Deploying from a GitHub repository to a service such as Railway or Render
Free plans have limits: read them first (some free services go to sleep when nobody visits)
Cloud basics with AWS: the free plan gives credits that run out, so read the terms first
Load balancers: why one server is not enough and how traffic is shared
Looking at logs and a health check after you deploy
checkpoint: Explain what an automatic check does when you push code.
Deploy the API with every secret set as an environment setting and none stored in the repository.
Explain why a free service may answer slowly after being idle, and say what the AWS free plan gives you and when it stops being free.

project.brief: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs your tests on every push. Then deploy the API to a service with a free or trial plan, after reading its limits, so that every setting, including the database address, comes from environment variables.

steps.title: Frontend Development
steps.goal: After this step you can build the screens of an app in React that load data from an API.
topics: Starting a project with Vite, a tool that runs and packs your project
Components, props and state in React
Hooks for loading data when a page opens
Moving between pages with a router
Showing loading and error messages
Talking to a backend API from the page
checkpoint: Build a page that loads a list from an API and shows loading and error states.
Explain what a component, a prop and state are.
Run the project with Vite, build it for production, and add a second page with a router.

project.brief: Build the front end of a notes app: a list page, an add form and a page for one note. Use fake data first, then a real API.

steps.title: Backend API
steps.goal: After this step you can build a set of web addresses (an API) with Express that the front end can ask for data.
topics: Starting an Express server
Routes: which code runs for which address and method
Reading request data: the address, the part after the question mark, and the message body
Middleware: small steps a request passes through
One error handler that sends clean error answers
Keeping routes in separate files with routers
checkpoint: Build create, read, update and delete routes with the right status codes.
Write a middleware and an error handler, and explain why the order matters.
Test each route by hand with Postman or curl.

project.brief: Build the notes API for your front end: list, create, edit and delete notes, with input checks and one error handler.

steps.title: Database Layer
steps.goal: After this step you can store your app's data in MongoDB, choose between embedding and linking, and ask questions across many records.
topics: Collections and documents in MongoDB
CRUD: create, read, update and delete
Mongoose models: a fixed shape for your data
Keeping related data inside one record, or in separate records that point to each other
Indexes: making searches fast
Aggregation: combining many records to get totals and counts
checkpoint: Design the models for a notes app with users and give the reason for each embed or link.
Add an index and explain what it speeds up and what it slows down.
Write a query that counts notes per user.

project.brief: Add MongoDB and Mongoose to your notes API: a User model and a Note model that belongs to a user, with one index and one count-per-user query.

steps.title: Full Stack Authentication
steps.goal: After this step you can add sign-in to a full stack app and explain how the site remembers who you are.
topics: Sessions: the server remembers you with a random ID
Cookies: the small piece of data the browser sends back each time
Cookie settings: Secure (only over HTTPS), HttpOnly (scripts cannot read it) and SameSite (stops other sites from sending your cookie)
Tokens (JWT): a signed note the browser carries instead of the server remembering you
OAuth 2.0: how "Sign in with Google" works without sharing your password
Signing out and session timeouts
Storing passwords safely: only a slow scrambled version, never the password
CORS: letting your front end on one address call your API on another
checkpoint: Explain what a session ID is and why it must be random and long.
Say what Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite each do for a cookie.
Log in as two users and show that one cannot read the other's notes.

project.brief: Add register, login and logout to your notes app. Keep the login in an HttpOnly cookie and let a user see only their own notes.

steps.title: State Management
steps.goal: After this step you can keep shared data in one place and choose between Context, Redux Toolkit and Zustand.
topics: Why shared state gets messy as an app grows
Context with a reducer: built into React
Redux Toolkit: one store, slices and async actions
Zustand: a small store without extra code
Choosing the simplest tool that works
checkpoint: Move the signed-in user into shared state.
Explain when Context is enough and when a store is worth adding.
Write one function that loads notes and stores them in shared state.

project.brief: Move the notes list and the signed-in user of your app into shared state, using Context with a reducer or Zustand.

steps.title: File Storage & Media
steps.goal: After this step you can let users upload files and store them in the cloud instead of on your own server.
topics: The file input in HTML and the File object
The accept setting is only a hint, so the server must check files too
Cloud storage (Amazon S3): folders called buckets that hold files
Firebase Storage and Cloudinary as easier options
Big files: uploading in chunks
Limits on file size and type
checkpoint: Build an upload form and show a preview of the chosen image.
Explain why the server must check the file type and size itself.
Say where uploaded files should live and why not on the app server.

project.brief: Add profile pictures to your app: pick a file, check its type and size on the server, upload it to cloud storage and show it.

steps.title: Testing & Debugging
steps.goal: After this step you can write tests for components and API routes and try an API by hand.
topics: Testing a React component by what the user sees (Testing Library)
The Vitest test runner, made for Vite projects
Testing API routes
Trying an API by hand with Postman
Reading error messages and using the browser's developer tools
checkpoint: Write a test that types in a form and checks the message shown.
Write a test for an API route that checks the status code and the data.
Use Postman to call a protected route with and without a login.

practice.label: Status codes you check in tests

project.brief: Write five tests for your notes app: two for components and three for API routes.

steps.title: Security & Performance
steps.goal: After this step you can name the main web security risks and use caching and speed measurements to make an app faster.
topics: The OWASP Top 10: the most common web security risks
Limiting how many requests one person can make (rate limiting)
HTTP caching: reusing answers instead of asking again
Core Web Vitals: loading speed, response time and layout jumps
Load balancing: sharing traffic between servers
checkpoint: Name three risks from the OWASP Top 10 and a defence for each.
Set cache headers so that a logo is reused but a user page is not shared.
Explain what a load balancer does.

project.brief: Add rate limiting to your login route, set cache headers on your static files and measure the Core Web Vitals before and after.

steps.title: Deployment & Scaling
steps.goal: After this step you can deploy the front end and the back end, use HTTPS, and explain in simple words what changes when more people use the app.
topics: Deploying a web service to Render and a site to Vercel
Environment settings for passwords and keys
HTTPS certificates: free ones from Let's Encrypt
Free plans have limits: some free services sleep when idle
A rented computer in the cloud (Amazon EC2), its starting copy and its firewall rules
What changes when more people use the app: more servers behind a load balancer
checkpoint: Deploy the API and the front end and connect them with environment settings.
Explain why a free service may answer slowly after being idle.
Say what an EC2 instance is in one sentence.

project.brief: Deploy your notes app: the API on Render and the React app on Vercel, with every secret set as an environment setting.

steps.title: Kotlin Basics
steps.goal: After this step you can write small Kotlin programs with functions, classes and coroutines.
topics: Variables, types and functions
Making decisions and repeating work
Classes and objects
Null safety: stopping the most common crash
Collections: lists, sets and maps
Coroutines: a way to do slow work without freezing the app
checkpoint: Write a class with properties and a function, and create two objects.
Explain what null safety means with one example.
Explain in simple words what a coroutine is for.

project.brief: Write a command-line program in Kotlin that keeps a list of expenses, adds new ones and prints the total.

steps.title: Android Fundamentals
steps.goal: After this step you can build a simple Android app with several screens and explain what happens when a screen opens, hides or closes.
topics: Setting up Android Studio and running a first app
Activities: one screen of an app
The lifecycle: what an activity does when it starts, pauses and stops
Saving state, so rotating the phone does not lose your data
Resources: texts, images and colors kept outside the code
ViewModel: holds the data of a screen so it survives rotation
checkpoint: Run your first app on an emulator (a pretend phone on your computer) or a real phone.
Name the main lifecycle steps of an activity and what each one is for.
Explain what happens to your data when the screen is rotated and how to keep it.

project.brief: Build a two-screen app: a list of items and a detail screen. Keep what the user typed when the phone is rotated.

steps.title: Modern UI with Compose
steps.goal: After this step you can build screens with Compose, keep their state correctly and move between them.
topics: Composables: functions that each draw a part of the screen
State: data that makes the screen update when it changes
remember and rememberSaveable: keeping state while the app runs and across rotation
State hoisting: keeping the data in the parent so the parts are easy to reuse
Navigation between screens
checkpoint: Build a screen with a text field and a button that updates the screen.
Explain what state hoisting means.
Move between two screens with Navigation Compose.

project.brief: Build a notes app in Compose with a list screen, an edit screen and navigation between them.

steps.title: Data Storage
steps.goal: After this step you can save app data on the phone with Room and keep settings with DataStore.
topics: Choosing where to store data: files, settings or a database
Room: a database made of entities (tables), DAOs (code that asks the database questions) and a database class
DataStore: saving small settings
Using stored data in Compose through a ViewModel (the part that holds the data of a screen)
Scoped storage: limits on which files an app can see
checkpoint: Save and read a list of items with Room.
Save a dark mode setting with DataStore.
Explain when to use a database and when to use DataStore.

project.brief: Make your notes app save notes in a Room database and remember the dark mode setting with DataStore.

steps.title: Networking & API Calls
steps.goal: After this step you can load data from a web API in your app without freezing the screen, and show errors.
topics: Permissions needed for internet access
Calling a web API and reading its JSON answer
Tools such as Retrofit and OkHttp that make web calls easier
Doing network work in the background so the screen does not freeze
Showing loading and error states
A repository: one place the app gets its data from
checkpoint: Load a list from a public API and show it.
Show an error message when the call fails.
Explain why network calls must not freeze the screen.

project.brief: Add a screen to your app that loads items from a public API, shows a loading indicator and shows an error with a retry button.

steps.title: Firebase Services
steps.goal: After this step you can add sign-in and a cloud database to an Android app with Firebase.
topics: Adding Firebase to an Android project
Firebase Authentication: sign-in without building your own server
Cloud Firestore: a cloud database of documents and collections
Live updates: the screen changes when data changes
Security rules: who may read and write what
Free plan limits: read them first
checkpoint: Sign a user in and show their name.
Save and read a document in Firestore.
Change a security rule and show that a read is now blocked.

project.brief: Add sign-in and a Firestore database to your notes app so each user sees only their own notes on any phone.

steps.title: Testing & Debugging
steps.goal: After this step you can write tests for your app, read Logcat to find problems and see crashes from real users.
topics: Local tests (fast, on your computer) and instrumented tests (tests that run on a phone)
UI tests that tap and check the screen
Logcat: the live log of your app
Log levels and filtering the log
Crashlytics: reports of crashes from real users
checkpoint: Write a local test for a function.
Filter Logcat to show only your app's errors.
Explain what Crashlytics shows you.

project.brief: Add three local tests to your app and set up Crashlytics. Force a test crash and find it in the console.

steps.title: Publishing
steps.goal: After this step you can sign your app and know what Google Play needs before you can publish it.
topics: The Play Console: where you manage your app
App signing: the key you prove you are the developer with, and the key Google uses to sign what users download
Keeping keys safe
Testing tracks: internal and closed testing
The testing rule for new personal accounts (Google changes it, so read the current help page)
Store listing and policies
checkpoint: Explain the difference between the key you upload with and the key Google signs with.
Say what a new personal developer account must do before it can publish.
Create a signed release build.

project.brief: Create a signed release build of your app and write the checklist you would follow to publish it on Google Play.

steps.title: Data Fundamentals
steps.goal: After this step you can explain what data analysis is, list its steps, and name common mistakes that give wrong answers.
topics: Kinds of data: numbers, categories and text
Rows, columns and tables
The steps of an analysis: ask, collect, clean, explore, build a prediction or summary, share
Describing data before drawing conclusions
Common mistakes: bias, mixing up fact and opinion, and misreading numbers
checkpoint: List the steps of a data analysis in order and say what happens in each.
Explain the difference between a number and a category with an example.
Name two mistakes that lead to a wrong conclusion (for example bias or misreading a chart) and describe a table with five numbers using only its average and its range.

project.brief: Pick a small public data table, describe each column in plain words, and write three questions the data could answer.

steps.title: Spreadsheet Skills (Excel)
steps.goal: After this step you can clean a table, use formulas and PivotTables, and make a chart in a spreadsheet.
topics: Cells, rows, columns and formatting
Formulas and functions such as IF, VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP
Sorting and filtering
PivotTables: summarising many rows in a small table
Charts
Removing duplicates and tidying messy text
Drop-down lists and data checks
checkpoint: Use a lookup formula to add a column from another table.
Build a PivotTable that adds up sales by month.
Make a chart and explain what it shows.

project.brief: Take a sales table, clean it, build a PivotTable of sales by month and a chart, and write three sentences about what you see.

steps.title: Python for Data Analytics
steps.goal: After this step you can load a table in pandas, filter it, group it and combine tables.
topics: Running Python in a notebook such as Jupyter or Google Colab
Python basics: variables, lists, functions
NumPy arrays: fast lists of numbers
pandas tables (DataFrames: tables in Python)
Selecting rows and columns

steps.title: Big O, Arrays and Hash Tables
steps.goal: After this step you can say how fast a piece of code grows as its input grows, and use arrays and hash tables to solve search and counting problems.
topics: Big O: a way to describe how the work grows when the input grows
Common growth rates: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n) and O(n squared)
Arrays: items kept in order and reached by their position
Adding at the end of a growing array is cheap when you count over many additions (amortized O(1)); adding at the front costs O(n)
Hash tables: look up an item by its key, O(1) on average with a good hash function, but O(n) in the worst case
Collisions: two keys landing in the same slot, and why they slow a hash table down
Counting and grouping with a hash table
Sets: a hash table that keeps only keys, to ask "have I seen this?" quickly

topics: Two pointers: two positions that move through a list, often from both ends of a sorted list
Finding a pair with a given sum in a sorted list in one pass
A fixed-size window: slide it one step and update the answer instead of starting again
A window that grows and shrinks to keep a rule true
Why one pass is O(n): each pointer only moves in one direction and never goes back, so there are at most about n moves in total (our own reasoning)
The smallest value in every window with a double-ended queue (deque)

steps.title: Sorting and Binary Search
steps.goal: After this step you can choose a sorting method, explain what makes a sort stable, and use binary search correctly, including on an answer range.
topics: Sorting: a method that only compares items cannot beat O(n log n) on average (counting sort and radix sort do not compare, so they can)
Merge sort: O(n log n) in every case, stable, needs extra memory. Heapsort: O(n log n) in every case, works in place, not stable

Quicksort: O(n log n) on average but O(n squared) in the worst case, and the usual in-place version is not stable. Insertion sort: O(n) at best (when the list is already sorted), O(n squared) on average, stable
Stable sort: items with equal keys keep their original order
Binary search: halve the search area each time, but the list must be sorted first and must allow jumping to the middle (an array, not a linked list)
With repeated values, finding the first or the last match needs a small change
Binary search on the answer: searching a range of possible answers instead of a list
checkpoint: Say why binary search needs a sorted list.
Explain the difference between a stable and an unstable sort with a small example.

steps.title: Linked Lists, Stacks and Queues
steps.goal: After this step you can build and use a linked list, a stack and a queue, and say what each one costs.
topics: Linked list: nodes that each point to the next one
A linked list is fast to add at the front (O(1)) but slow to reach a position (O(n))
A cycle in a linked list (a node that points back to an earlier one) makes a loop run forever, so check for it
Stack: last in, first out (push and pop at one end); taking from an empty stack or queue is called underflow
Queue: first in, first out (add at the back, remove from the front, both O(1) when it keeps track of its back end or uses a deque)
Python's deque: fast at both ends, unlike removing from the front of a list (O(n))
A stack that also knows its smallest item in O(1)
Fast and slow pointers: one pointer moves two steps while another moves one, and they meet if there is a cycle

steps.title: Recursion and Backtracking
steps.goal: After this step you can write a recursive function and use backtracking to list all the ways to build an answer.
topics: Recursion: a function that calls itself on a smaller problem, with a base case that stops it
Backtracking: build the answer one choice at a time and drop a choice as soon as it cannot lead to a solution
Checking early (pruning) can save a lot of work, but the worst case stays the same
If nothing is ever rejected, backtracking is just trying everything (brute force)
Total work is roughly the number of choices in the search tree times the work per choice

steps.title: Trees and Binary Search Trees
steps.goal: After this step you can walk through a tree in four ways and use a binary search tree, and you know when it becomes slow.
topics: Trees: a root, parents and children
Walking through a tree: pre-order, in-order, post-order (depth first) and level order (breadth first)
Depth first uses a stack or recursion; level order uses a queue
Binary search tree: every key in the left part of a node is smaller and every key in the right part is bigger, not only its direct children
A binary search tree searches in O(log n) on average (for example when keys arrive in random order) but O(n) in the worst case; walking it in-order gives the keys sorted
Inserting keys in sorted order turns the tree into a linked list
Balanced trees keep the height at O(log n)
Very deep recursion can hit a language's depth limit
checkpoint: Write the four walking orders for a small tree you draw yourself.
Explain why inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order into a binary search tree gives a tall tree like a linked list.
Check whether a tree is a valid binary search tree.

steps.title: Heaps and Tries
steps.goal: After this step you can use a heap as a priority queue and a trie to store and search words.
topics: Binary heap: a tree filled level by level from the left where no parent is larger than its children (a min-heap)
Finding the smallest is O(1); removing it is O(log n); adding is O(log n) in the worst case
Building a heap from a list is O(n); adding the items one by one is O(n log n)
A heap is not sorted, so searching for any value is still O(n)
Priority queue: serve the most important item first, and the heap is the usual way to build one
Python's heapq and Java's PriorityQueue
Trie: a tree where each step is one letter
Finding a word in a trie takes O(m) for a word of m letters, if each letter's link can be found in constant time, but its links can use a lot of memory

steps.title: Graphs: Walking Through a Network
steps.goal: After this step you can store a graph and walk through it with breadth-first and depth-first search.
topics: Graphs: nodes (vertices) and the lines between them (edges)
Storing a graph: an adjacency list (for each node, the list of its neighbours) or an adjacency matrix (a table of yes or no for every pair of nodes)
Breadth-first search (BFS): layer by layer with a queue, and when edges have no costs it finds the fewest edges from the start to every node
Depth-first search (DFS): as deep as possible, then step back, with a stack or recursion
Both take O(V + E) with an adjacency list: the number of nodes plus the number of edges (with an adjacency matrix it is O(V squared))
Keep a record of visited nodes, or a cycle makes DFS run forever
Topological sort: ordering tasks so each one comes after the ones it needs, only possible for a directed graph with no cycle, in O(V + E)

steps.title: Graphs: Shortest Paths and Spanning Trees
steps.goal: After this step you can find cheapest routes with Dijkstra, join groups with union-find, and build a minimum spanning tree with Kruskal.
topics: Weighted graphs: each edge has a cost
Dijkstra's algorithm: the cheapest route from one start to every node, when no edge cost is negative
Dijkstra with a binary heap takes O((E + V) log V)
With a negative edge cost Dijkstra can give a wrong answer; Bellman-Ford handles negative costs but takes O(V times E)

Union-find (disjoint sets): quickly tell whether two items are in the same group; with both path compression and union by rank each step costs amortized O(alpha(n)), a number that grows so slowly that it stays tiny in practice
Minimum spanning tree: connect all nodes of an undirected graph with the smallest total cost (this is not the same as the shortest routes)
Kruskal's algorithm: take the cheapest edge that does not make a cycle, O(E log E) because of the sorting
checkpoint: Explain why Dijkstra needs non-negative edge costs.
Say what union-find does and why path compression and union by rank make it fast.

steps.goal: After this step you can tell when a greedy method is correct, and solve interval problems such as scheduling the most meetings.

A greedy method is not always correct, so it needs a reason (a proof)
Fractional knapsack is solved exactly by greedy; 0/1 knapsack is not
Interval scheduling: to fit the most meetings, always pick the meeting that ends first among those that do not overlap the ones already chosen (O(n log n) with the sorting)
Other rules such as earliest start or shortest meeting can give a wrong answer
Merging overlapping intervals (this one sorts by start time, a different order)

steps.title: Dynamic Programming
steps.goal: After this step you can spot a dynamic programming problem, write it with memoization or a table, and say its cost.
topics: Dynamic programming: split a problem into smaller problems that repeat, and solve each only once
It needs two things: the best answer is built from best answers of smaller parts, and the small problems repeat
Merge sort and quicksort are not dynamic programming because their small problems do not repeat
Memoization: remember each answer so the same call is never computed twice (only for functions that always give the same answer for the same input)
Top down (with memoization) and bottom up (filling a table)
Example: Fibonacci takes O(n) time with memoization and can use O(1) space bottom up
0/1 knapsack: O(n times W) time, which grows with the capacity W, not only with the number of items
Longest increasing subsequence: O(n squared) with a simple table, O(n log n) with a binary-search method

AND, OR, XOR and NOT on bits, and shifting bits left or right

Compiling, testing and packaging with Maven commands
Adding libraries as dependencies
JUnit: the platform and the Jupiter way of writing tests (the current JUnit needs Java 17 or later)
Writing a test: annotations and assertions, including checking that an error is thrown
Setup and cleanup methods
checkpoint: Create a Maven project, add one dependency and run its tests from the command line.
Write three JUnit tests for one class, including one that expects an error.
Explain what the pom.xml file is for.

project.brief: Turn your library program into a Maven project and write ten JUnit tests for it.

steps.title: Spring Core and Spring Boot
steps.goal: After this step you can create a Spring Boot project, explain what dependency injection is, and run your app.
topics: Inversion of control: the container creates your objects and hands them what they need
Dependency injection: a class lists what it needs and Spring supplies it
Beans: objects that the Spring container creates and manages
Spring Boot: stand-alone apps that you just run, with a server built in
Starters and auto-configuration: ready-made settings so you write less setup
Spring Initializr: a tool that generates a starter project
Production features: health checks, metrics and settings kept outside the code
checkpoint: Explain dependency injection to a friend in three sentences.
Generate a Spring Boot project (it needs Java 17 or later), run it and see it start in the console.
Say what auto-configuration does and why it helps.

project.brief: Generate a Spring Boot project and add two classes where one needs the other, so that Spring connects them for you (dependency injection). Print a message when the app starts, with a small piece of code that runs at startup.

steps.title: Building a REST API with Spring MVC
steps.goal: After this step you can build a REST API with Spring Boot that returns JSON and uses the right status codes.
topics: Spring MVC: controllers receive web requests
@RestController, @GetMapping and @RequestMapping: which code answers which address
Reading input with @RequestParam
Creating, changing and deleting with @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PathVariable and @RequestBody
A record or class that becomes the JSON answer
Running the service as one executable JAR and testing it
HTTP methods and status codes: 200, 201, 204, 400 and 404
checkpoint: Create a route that returns a greeting as JSON and takes an optional name.
Add create, read, update and delete routes with correct status codes.
Test each route with curl or Postman.

project.brief: Build a to-do list API with Spring Boot: list, add, finish and delete items, kept in memory for now. Return 404 when an item does not exist.

steps.title: Databases with Spring Data JPA
steps.goal: After this step you can save and read data from a database with Spring Data JPA and set up a database connection.
topics: Settings for a database connection (spring.datasource) and an embedded test database
Connection pooling: reusing database connections
Entities: a Java class that becomes a table (@Entity, @Id, @GeneratedValue)
Repositories: ready-made save, find and delete methods
Query methods: write a method name such as findByLastName and Spring builds the query
Transactions: a group of changes that all happen or none happen
Keeping data after a restart: the small built-in test database lives in memory, so use a file-based or server database such as MySQL or PostgreSQL
checkpoint: Create an entity and a repository and save three records.
Write a query method that finds records by one field.
Explain what a transaction guarantees.

project.brief: Add a database to your to-do API: store items with Spring Data JPA in a database that keeps its data after a restart (add the JPA starter and your database's driver), and add a query that finds the unfinished items.

steps.title: Securing the App with Spring Security
steps.goal: After this step you can add sign-in to a Spring Boot app, store passwords safely and explain what the main protections do.
topics: Authentication: proving who you are
Authorization: deciding what each person may do
Form login and a login page
Passwords: store only a hash, a one-way fingerprint that cannot be turned back (for example BCrypt), never the password
A security filter chain: which addresses are public and which need a login
CSRF and security headers: protections Spring Security turns on for you
OAuth 2.0 login (for example "Sign in with Google") and tokens: Spring Security supports them, and you only need to know where they fit
checkpoint: Protect one route so that only a signed-in user can open it.
Explain why passwords are stored as a BCrypt hash and not as plain text.
Say what CSRF is in one sentence and what protects you.

project.brief: Add sign-in to your to-do API (HTTP Basic or a login form) so that each user sees only their own items. Keep users in the database with BCrypt-hashed passwords.

steps.title: Testing and Packaging with Docker
steps.goal: After this step you can write tests for a Spring Boot app and run it in a Docker container.
topics: spring-boot-starter-test: JUnit, AssertJ and Hamcrest in one package
Testing a Spring Boot application: starting it in a test and calling your routes
Testcontainers: tests that start real services in containers (Docker must be installed and running)
A Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app
Running as a non-root user in a container
Layered JARs for faster image builds
Spring profiles: different settings for different places
checkpoint: Write a test that calls one route and checks the answer.
Build a Docker image of the app and run it.
Explain what a Spring profile is for.

project.brief: Add tests to your to-do API and build a Docker image of it. Start the container and check that the API answers.

steps.title: Git and GitHub
steps.goal: After this step you can save your work with Git, work on branches, and share code on GitHub.
topics: Setting up Git and the basic commands: init, add, commit, clone, pull and push
Git keeps snapshots of your project, not just differences
Nearly every Git action happens on your own computer
The three states of a file: modified, staged and committed
Branches: working on a change without touching the main code
Remote repositories and GitHub (you need a free account)
Merging and fixing conflicts
.gitignore (files Git should skip) and pull requests (asking to merge your branch)
checkpoint: Create a repository, make three commits and read the history.
Create a branch, change a file and merge it back.
Push a project to GitHub.

project.brief: Put one of your projects on GitHub with a README, work on a new feature in a branch and merge it.

steps.title: Linux and the Command Line
steps.goal: After this step you can move around a Linux system, work with files and permissions, and manage programs from the command line.
topics: The command line and moving around the file system
Reading and searching text files
Users and file permissions
Processes: seeing what is running and stopping it
Installing software with a package manager
Simple shell scripts: running several commands from a file
Looking things up: the manual pages, and the logs where programs write what they do
Getting a Linux system to practise on: a virtual machine, or the Windows Subsystem for Linux on Windows
checkpoint: Create a folder, a file and a script, and make the script runnable.
Find a process and stop it.
Read the manual page of a command you have not used before.

project.brief: Write a shell script that backs up a folder into a dated archive and run it by hand on a Linux machine or a virtual machine.

steps.title: Networking for DevOps
steps.goal: After this step you can explain addresses, ports, DNS and HTTP, and the parts of a cloud network.
topics: IP addresses, subnets (smaller networks inside a network) and private ranges
Ports and sockets: the numbered doors a program listens on
DNS: how a name becomes an address
HTTP and HTTPS
Load balancers, proxies and CDNs (spreading traffic over servers, hiding servers, and keeping copies of files near users)
A cloud network (a VPC): subnets, routing and gateways
Firewalls and security groups: rules about who may connect
Finding network problems with simple tools such as ping, curl and dig
checkpoint: Say which of 10.0.0.5 and 172.32.0.1 is a private address and why.
Explain what a subnet is and what a route does.
Follow a request from a browser to a server through DNS, a load balancer and an app.

project.brief: Draw the network of a small web app (a user, DNS, a load balancer, two servers and a database) and write what each arrow carries.

steps.title: Docker and Containers
steps.goal: After this step you can build an image, run containers with ports, volumes and settings, and start several containers together with Compose.
topics: What Docker is: a platform for building, shipping and running apps in containers (install Docker Desktop or Docker Engine first)
Images and containers
docker run: ports, volumes, environment settings and background mode
Building images with a Dockerfile and BuildKit
Docker Compose: several containers described in one file
Looking inside a running container: docker ps, logs and exec
Registries: storing images on a service such as Docker Hub
checkpoint: Run a container in the background with a port linked to your computer.
Write a Dockerfile for a small app and build it.
Start an app and its database together with Compose.

project.brief: Pack a small web app and its database with Docker Compose, so that one command starts both.

steps.title: Automatic Checks with GitHub Actions
steps.goal: After this step you can write a workflow that builds and tests your code automatically on every push.
topics: Continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD): building, testing and releasing automatically
Workflows: files in .github/workflows that describe the steps
Events: what starts a workflow
Jobs and steps, and running them on a runner
Reusing ready-made actions
Building and testing code in your language
Reading the results on the Actions tab
Secrets and limits: keep passwords out of workflow files, and check the free minutes on the pricing page
checkpoint: Write a workflow that runs your tests on every push.
Make a test fail on purpose and find it in the Actions tab.
Explain what an event, a job and a runner are.

project.brief: Add a GitHub Actions workflow to one of your earlier projects that has tests, so that it installs the project, runs its tests and shows a failed build when a test fails.

steps.title: Cloud Basics with AWS
steps.goal: After this step you can explain the main AWS services (IAM, EC2 and S3), start a server, store files and control who can do what.
topics: IAM: who you are (authentication) and what you may do (authorization)
EC2: a rented computer in the cloud with machine images (AMIs), instance types, disks, key pairs and security groups
S3: storage in buckets that hold objects
How cloud services are billed: pay for what you use; the free offer for new accounts changes, so read the current pricing page
Regions: where in the world your service runs
Root user and other identities: do daily work with a separate user, and give each person or program only what it needs
Billing alerts: set a budget alert before you start anything
checkpoint: Say the difference between authentication and authorization.
Explain what a security group does for an EC2 server.
Say how you would avoid a surprise bill when you practise.

project.brief: Within the free limits, start one small server (open port 80 in its security group and install a web server), put a file in a storage bucket, then delete everything and check the billing page. Public IPv4 addresses can cost money, so check that too.

steps.title: Kubernetes and Terraform
steps.goal: After this step you can explain what Kubernetes and Terraform are for and run a first example of each.
topics: Why Kubernetes exists: running and managing many containers
What Kubernetes is not: not a platform that builds your code and not a bundled database
The Kubernetes basics tutorial: create a cluster (a practice cluster on your own computer), deploy an app, explore it, open it to the world, scale it and update it
The main objects: a Pod runs your containers, a Deployment keeps them running, a Service gives them one address
Infrastructure as code: describing servers and networks in files
Terraform: write the plan, check it and apply it
State: how Terraform remembers what it built
Cleaning up: terraform destroy removes what Terraform built
checkpoint: Explain in your own words why a team would use Kubernetes.
Deploy and scale a sample app in a practice cluster.
Say what the three steps write, plan and apply do in Terraform.

project.brief: Follow the Kubernetes basics tutorial in a practice cluster, then write a small Terraform file that creates one harmless local resource (for example a text file) so that no cloud account or payment is needed, and destroy it afterwards.

steps.title: Monitoring and Reliability
steps.goal: After this step you can collect metrics, draw a dashboard, and explain what monitoring, alerts and post-incident reviews are for.
topics: Metrics: numbers that describe your system over time
Prometheus: an open-source monitoring and alerting toolkit
A pull model: Prometheus asks each service for its numbers over HTTP, so your app must serve a page of numbers (a library helps)
PromQL: the query language for asking Prometheus for numbers
Grafana: dashboards built on top of data sources such as Prometheus
Alerts: telling a person when something needs attention
Logs: treating what a program prints as a stream of events
checkpoint: Run Prometheus and Grafana and show one number on a dashboard.
Explain the difference between a metric and a log line.
Write what you would check first when a chart goes red.

project.brief: Add a metrics page to a small app with a Prometheus library, collect it with Prometheus, draw two charts in Grafana with PromQL and set one alert rule.

steps.title: Capstone: Ship an App End to End
steps.goal: After this step you can take an app from code on GitHub to a running, tested and monitored service, and explain each part.
topics: The twelve-factor app: twelve simple rules for apps that are easy to run and move
Codebase, dependencies and config kept in the right places
Backing services such as databases treated as attached resources
Build, release and run as separate stages
Processes, port binding, concurrency and disposability
Logs and admin tasks
Writing down how it works so someone else can run it
checkpoint: Name at least six of the twelve factors and say what each one asks of your app.
Show your pipeline from a code push to a running service.
Show a dashboard and say what you would check first if it went red.

project.brief: Take one app and ship it end to end: code on GitHub, tests in GitHub Actions, a Docker image that runs with Compose on your own computer (no paid cloud is needed; you may also use a free plan), and metrics on a dashboard. Write a one-page guide so someone else can run it.
